newsitem.title: USA: Low-tech Court confronts high-tech Internet culture.
newsitem.headline: Low-tech Court confronts high-tech Internet culture.

text.p: Just moments after the Supreme Court issued its landmark ruling on Internet free speech Thursday, Jonah Seiger was crouched outside the court with his laptop computer and cellular phone.

Propping himself in a shady spot to avoid the beating sun, Seiger popped a floppy disk into his computer, initiated a call by cellular modem and within two minutes had transferred an electronic copy of the historic decision to a computer connected to the Internet.

"Immediately, it's available all over the world to everyone," said Seiger, occasional poster boy for the growing Internet lobby and full-time communications director at the Center for Democracy and Technology here.
Even before the text went online, Seiger had signaled his webmaster to alert millions of Internet users that the court had decided to overturn the Communications Decency Act.

In typical Internet fashion, the signal came in the form of a small graphic image displayed on 12,000 web sites. The animated picture, which for weeks had asked "Will online free speech survive," was changed to "Victory in the Supreme Court -- online free speech will survive."
The high-tech scene provided a stark contrast with the goings on inside the court.

Following time-honored procedures, court workers in the public affairs office greeted reporters on Thursday morning with a closed paper box filled with copies of the rulings to be handed down that day.

Reporters are not told which rulings will be delivered on any particular day, but with the court's term winding down and only five cases remaining, most people expected to get the Internet decision on Thursday.
At 10 a.m. EDT/1400 GMT, the public affairs office received a call from the court for permission to distribute the first decision of the day.
"Ninety-five dash 511," the clerk answering the phone called out, referring to the docket number of the decision to be given out first.
"That's it," one reporter squealed, as journalists for wire services, newspapers and radio and television stations grabbed for copies of the 40-page decision.

Usually, the court distributes its decisions only in paper form, but Seiger and a few other parties had asked that the first ruling about the digital world also be provided in digital form -- on a floppy disk.
"The court made a special exception for this case," he said.
